claim: ADAR1 isoforms are adenosine deaminases that edit and destabilize double-stranded RNA reducing its immunostimulatory activities.
source: ADAR1 isoforms are adenosine deaminases that edit and destabilize double-stranded RNA reducing its immunostimulatory activities.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about ADAR1 function.

claim: Mutation of ADAR1 leads to Aicardi-Goutiéres syndrome, a severe neurodevelopmental and inflammatory disease of children.
source: Mutation of ADAR1 leads to a severe neurodevelopmental and inflammatory disease of children, Aicardi-Goutiéres syndrome.
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Rice et al., 2012 in the Introduction section.

claim: Adar1 mutations are embryonic lethal in mice.
source: In mice, Adar1 mutations are embryonic lethal but are rescued by mutation of the Mda5 or Mavs genes, which function in IFN induction.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Pestal et al., 2015; Liddicoat et al., 2015; Mannion et al., 2014 in the manuscript.

claim: Adar1 embryonic lethality in mice is rescued by mutation of the Mda5 or Mavs genes.
source: In mice, Adar1 mutations are embryonic lethal but are rescued by mutation of the Mda5 or Mavs genes, which function in IFN induction.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Pestal et al., 2015; Liddicoat et al., 2015; Mannion et al., 2014.

claim: The cell-lethal phenotype of ADAR1 deletion in human lung adenocarcinoma A549 cells is rescued by CRISPR/Cas9 mutagenesis of the RNASEL gene.
source: We show that the cell-lethal phenotype of ADAR1 deletion in human lung adenocarcinoma A549 cells is rescued by CRISPR/Cas9 mutagenesis of the RNASEL gene or by expression of the RNase L antagonist, murine coronavirus NS2 accessory protein.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Table 3 and Figure 2.

claim: The cell-lethal phenotype of ADAR1 deletion in A549 cells is rescued by expression of the RNase L antagonist, murine coronavirus NS2 accessory protein.
source: We show that the cell-lethal phenotype of ADAR1 deletion in human lung adenocarcinoma A549 cells is rescued by CRISPR/Cas9 mutagenesis of the RNASEL gene or by expression of the RNase L antagonist, murine coronavirus NS2 accessory protein.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Table 3 and Figure 5.

claim: Ablation of RNase L activity promotes survival of ADAR1 deficient cells even in the presence of MDA5 and MAVS.
source: Our result demonstrate that ablation of RNase L activity promotes survival of ADAR1 deficient cells even in the presence of MDA5 and MAVS, suggesting that the RNase L system is the primary sensor pathway for endogenous dsRNA that leads to cell death.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing that RNASEL-ADAR1 DKO cells are viable while maintaining MAVS expression (Table 3, Figure 2, Figure 4).

claim: The RNase L system is the primary sensor pathway for endogenous dsRNA that leads to cell death.
source: Our result demonstrate that ablation of RNase L activity promotes survival of ADAR1 deficient cells even in the presence of MDA5 and MAVS, suggesting that the RNase L system is the primary sensor pathway for endogenous dsRNA that leads to cell death.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental results showing that RNase L ablation rescues ADAR1 deficiency even when MAVS is present.

claim: ADAR1 converts adenosine to inosine (A-to-I editing) in dsRNA.
source: Adenosine deaminase acting on dsRNA (ADAR1) isoforms neutralize the immunostimulatory activity of double-stranded RNA (dsRNA) by converting adenosine to inosine (i.e., A-to-I editing) (George et al., 2014; Tomaselli et al., 2015; Patterson and Samuel, 1995).
evidence: This is supported by citations to George et al., 2014; Tomaselli et al., 2015; Patterson and Samuel, 1995.

claim: ADAR1 destabilizes dsRNA because A:U base pairs are stronger than I:U mismatches.
source: ADAR1 alters the RNA coding sequence, because I is read as G, and it also destabilizes dsRNA because A:U base pairs are disrupted than I:U mismatches.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge of RNA base pairing.

claim: ADAR1 modifications suppress cellular responses to dsRNA and prevent type I IFN production.
source: These modifications by ADAR1 suppress the cellular responses to dsRNA and prevent to type I IFN production.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge of ADAR1 function.

claim: There are three mammalian ADAR genes (ADAR1-3).
source: There are three mammalian ADAR genes (ADAR1-3), but only ADAR1 isoforms p110 and p150 and ADAR2 have deaminase activity (Tomaselli et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Tomaselli et al., 2015.

claim: Only ADAR1 isoforms p110 and p150 and ADAR2 have deaminase activity.
source: There are three mammalian ADAR genes (ADAR1-3), but only ADAR1 isoforms p110 and p150 and ADAR2 have deaminase activity (Tomaselli et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Tomaselli et al., 2015.

claim: ADAR1 p150 isoform is IFN inducible.
source: The IFN inducible ADAR1 p150 isoform (subsequently 'p150') is present in both the cytoplasm and nucleus, while the constitutive ADAR1 p110 (an N-terminal truncated isoform translated from a shorter mRNA initiated at a downstream promoter in ADAR1) and ADAR2 are mostly nuclear.
evidence: This is established knowledge about ADAR1 isoforms.

claim: ADAR1 p150 is present in both the cytoplasm and nucleus.
source: The IFN inducible ADAR1 p150 isoform (subsequently 'p150') is present in both the cytoplasm and nucleus, while the constitutive ADAR1 p110 (an N-terminal truncated isoform translated from a shorter mRNA initiated at a downstream promoter in ADAR1) and ADAR2 are mostly nuclear.
evidence: This is established knowledge about ADAR1 subcellular localization.

claim: ADAR1 p110 is constitutively expressed and mostly nuclear.
source: The IFN inducible ADAR1 p150 isoform (subsequently 'p150') is present in both the cytoplasm and nucleus, while the constitutive ADAR1 p110 (an N-terminal truncated isoform translated from a shorter mRNA initiated at a downstream promoter in ADAR1) and ADAR2 are mostly nuclear.
evidence: This is established knowledge about ADAR1 p110.

claim: ADAR1 p110 is an N-terminal truncated isoform translated from a shorter mRNA initiated at a downstream promoter in ADAR1.
source: The IFN inducible ADAR1 p150 isoform (subsequently 'p150') is present in both the cytoplasm and nucleus, while the constitutive ADAR1 p110 (an N-terminal truncated isoform translated from a shorter mRNA initiated at a downstream promoter in ADAR1) and ADAR2 are mostly nuclear.
evidence: This is established knowledge about ADAR1 p110 structure.

claim: ADAR2 is mostly nuclear.
source: The IFN inducible ADAR1 p150 isoform (subsequently 'p150') is present in both the cytoplasm and nucleus, while the constitutive ADAR1 p110 (an N-terminal truncated isoform translated from a shorter mRNA initiated at a downstream promoter in ADAR1) and ADAR2 are mostly nuclear.
evidence: This is established knowledge about ADAR2 localization.

claim: Mutations of ADAR1 result in Aicardi-Goutiéres syndrome.
source: Mutations of ADAR1 result in the severe, sometimes lethal, childhood neurodevelopmental disease, Aicardi-Goutiéres syndrome (Rice et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Rice et al., 2012.

claim: ADAR1 can be either pro-viral or anti-viral depending on the virus-host cell context.
source: Interestingly, ADAR1 can be either pro-viral or anti-viral depending on the virus-host cell context (reviewed in [George et al., 2014]).
evidence: This is supported by citation to George et al., 2014.

claim: The antiviral effects of ADAR1 are due to hyper-editing and mutagenesis of viral RNAs.
source: The antiviral effects are due to hyper-editing and mutagenesis of viral RNAs (Samuel, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Samuel, 2011.

claim: Proviral effects of ADAR1 are due in part to editing of viral RNAs.
source: Proviral effects are due in part to editing of viral RNAs (Wong and Lazinski, 2002) and/or to destabilizing dsRNA resulting in suppression of dsRNA-signaling through MDA5 and MAVS to type I IFN genes (Figure 1).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Wong and Lazinski, 2002.

claim: Proviral effects of ADAR1 are due to destabilizing dsRNA resulting in suppression of dsRNA-signaling through MDA5 and MAVS to type I IFN genes.
source: Proviral effects are due in part to editing of viral RNAs (Wong and Lazinski, 2002) and/or to destabilizing dsRNA resulting in suppression of dsRNA-signaling through MDA5 and MAVS to type I IFN genes (Figure 1).
evidence: This is supported by inference from the mechanism shown in Figure 1.

claim: Mutation of either MDA5 or MAVS rescues the embryonic lethal phenotype of Adar1 knockout mice.
source: Accordingly, mutation of either MDA5 or MAVS rescues the embryonic lethal phenotype of Adar1 knockout (KO) mice (Pestal et al., 2015; Liddicoat et al., 2015; Mannion et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Pestal et al., 2015; Liddicoat et al., 2015; Mannion et al., 2014.

claim: ADAR1 antagonizes the IFN-inducible dsRNA-dependent serine/threonine protein kinase, PKR.
source: ADAR1 also antagonizes the IFN-inducible dsRNA-dependent serine/threonine protein kinase, PKR, presumably by altering the structure of dsRNA and thereby preventing both PKR activation and phosphorylation of its substrate protein, eIF2α (Samuel, 2011; Gélinas et al., 2011; Wang et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Samuel, 2011; Gélinas et al., 2011; Wang et al., 2004.

claim: ADAR1 prevents PKR activation by altering the structure of dsRNA.
source: ADAR1 also antagonizes the IFN-inducible dsRNA-dependent serine/threonine protein kinase, PKR, presumably by altering the structure of dsRNA and thereby preventing both PKR activation and phosphorylation of its substrate protein, eIF2α (Samuel, 2011; Gélinas et al., 2011; Wang et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Samuel, 2011; Gélinas et al., 2011; Wang et al., 2004.

claim: OAS isoforms (OAS1, OAS2, OAS3) are IFN inducible enzymes that sense dsRNA and produce 2',5'-oligoadenylates (2-5A).
source: OAS isoforms (OAS1, OAS2, OAS3) are IFN inducible enzymes that sense dsRNA and produce 2',5'-oligoadenylates (2-5A) which activate RNase L to degrade viral and host single-stranded RNAs leading to apoptosis and inhibition of virus growth (Silverman and Weiss, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Silverman and Weiss, 2014.

claim: 2-5A activates RNase L to degrade viral and host single-stranded RNAs leading to apoptosis and inhibition of virus growth.
source: OAS isoforms (OAS1, OAS2, OAS3) are IFN inducible enzymes that sense dsRNA and produce 2',5'-oligoadenylates (2-5A) which activate RNase L to degrade viral and host single-stranded RNAs leading to apoptosis and inhibition of virus growth (Silverman and Weiss, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Silverman and Weiss, 2014.

claim: ADAR1 single gene KO A549 cells were not viable.
source: Here we report that whereas ADAR1 single gene KO A549 cells were not viable, it was possible to rescue ADAR1 deficient cells by knockout (KO) of either RNASEL or MAVS or by expression of a viral antagonist of the OAS/RNase L system (Silverman and Weiss, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Table 3.

claim: It was possible to rescue ADAR1 deficient cells by knockout of either RNASEL or MAVS.
source: Here we report that whereas ADAR1 single gene KO A549 cells were not viable, it was possible to rescue ADAR1 deficient cells by knockout (KO) of either RNASEL or MAVS or by expression of a viral antagonist of the OAS/RNase L system (Silverman and Weiss, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Table 3 and Figure 2.

claim: It was possible to rescue ADAR1 deficient cells by expression of a viral antagonist of the OAS/RNase L system.
source: Here we report that whereas ADAR1 single gene KO A549 cells were not viable, it was possible to rescue ADAR1 deficient cells by knockout (KO) of either RNASEL or MAVS or by expression of a viral antagonist of the OAS/RNase L system (Silverman and Weiss, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Table 3 and Figure 5.

claim: RNase L activation is the primary mode of cell death induced by either endogenous or exogenous dsRNA.
source: Our results suggest that the RNase L activation is the primary mode of cell death induced by either endogenous or exogenous dsRNA.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental results showing that RNase L ablation protects cells from dsRNA-induced death.

claim: Cells lacking RNase L expression were resistant to cell death at treatment with up to 5 µg/ml of pIC.
source: Cells lacking RNase L expression were resistant to cell death at treatment with up to 5 µg/ml of pIC while treatment of WT A549 as well as PKR KO or MAVS KO cells with 0.5 µg/ml of pIC promoted cell death (Figure 3a).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3a.

claim: Treatment of WT A549 as well as PKR KO or MAVS KO cells with 0.5 µg/ml of pIC promoted cell death.
source: Cells lacking RNase L expression were resistant to cell death at treatment with up to 5 µg/ml of pIC while treatment of WT A549 as well as PKR KO or MAVS KO cells with 0.5 µg/ml of pIC promoted cell death (Figure 3a).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3a.

claim: Cells expressing RNase L died by 24–30 hr post treatment with pIC.
source: While cells expressing RNase L died by 24–30 hr post treatment, cells ablated for RNase L expression (RNASEL KO and RNASEL-MAVS DKO) were resistant to pIC induced cell death (Figure 3b&c).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3b and 3c.

claim: Cells ablated for RNase L expression (RNASEL KO and RNASEL-MAVS DKO) were resistant to pIC induced cell death.
source: While cells expressing RNase L died by 24–30 hr post treatment, cells ablated for RNase L expression (RNASEL KO and RNASEL-MAVS DKO) were resistant to pIC induced cell death (Figure 3b&c).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3b and 3c.

claim: RNASEL KO or RNASEL-MAVS DKO showed accelerated wound healing in monolayer scratch assays compared with MAVS KO and WT cells.
source: Similarly, RNASEL KO or RNASEL-MAVS DKO showed accelerated wound healing in monolayer scratch assays compared with MAVS KO and WT cells, all of which retained RNase L (Figure 3d).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3d.

claim: RNase L impairs cell migration in monolayer scratch assays.
source: RNase L was previously reported to impair cell migration in these assays (Banerjee et al., 2015; Rath et al., 2015) as well as to promote apoptosis (Zhou et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Banerjee et al., 2015; Rath et al., 2015.

claim: RNase L promotes apoptosis.
source: RNase L was previously reported to impair cell migration in these assays (Banerjee et al., 2015; Rath et al., 2015) as well as to promote apoptosis (Zhou et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Zhou et al., 1997.

claim: The protective effect of RNASEL KO was not restricted to A549 cells as human mammary epithelial (HME) cells were also protected from pIC-induced cell death by ablation of RNase L expression.
source: Finally, the protective effect of RNASEL KO was not restricted to A549 cells as human mammary epithelial (HME) cells were also protected from pIC-induced cell death by ablation of RNase L expression (Figure 3e).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3e.

claim: More than 40 clones derived from WT A549 cells or PKR KO A549 were screened and none had a KO of ADAR1.
source: Using lentivirus delivered CRISPR/Cas9 and sgRNA4 directed at Exon 1 of ADAR1 within the coding regions of p110 and p150 (Table 1; Figure 2—figure supplement 1) we screened more than 40 clones derived from WT A549 cells or PKR KO A549 and were unable to recover cells with a KO of ADAR1 (Table 3).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Table 3.

claim: Using RNASEL KO or MAVS KO A549 cells and lentivirus delivery of sgRNA4, both RNASEL-ADAR1 and MAVS-ADAR1 double KO cells were recovered.
source: However using RNASEL KO or MAVS KO A549 cells and similar lentivirus delivery of sgRNA4 we were able to recover both RNASEL-ADAR1 and MAVS-ADAR1 double KO (DKO) cells (Table 3, Figure 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Table 3 and Figure 2.

claim: MAVS-ADAR1 DKO cells died more slowly than WT cells following pIC transfection.
source: While MAVS-ADAR1 DKO cells died more slowly than WT cells, RNase L-ADAR1 DKO cells were almost completely protected from cell death further supporting the finding that RNase L is the major pathway leading to cell death in the absence of ADAR1 editing.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4a.

claim: RNase L-ADAR1 DKO cells were almost completely protected from cell death following pIC transfection.
source: While MAVS-ADAR1 DKO cells died more slowly than WT cells, RNase L-ADAR1 DKO cells were almost completely protected from cell death further supporting the finding that RNase L is the major pathway leading to cell death in the absence of ADAR1 editing.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4a.

claim: RNase L is the major pathway leading to cell death in the absence of ADAR1 editing.
source: While MAVS-ADAR1 DKO cells died more slowly than WT cells, RNase L-ADAR1 DKO cells were almost completely protected from cell death further supporting the finding that RNase L is the major pathway leading to cell death in the absence of ADAR1 editing.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing differential protection in MAVS-ADAR1 DKO vs RNASEL-ADAR1 DKO cells.

claim: WT RNase L expression in RNASEL-ADAR1 DKO caused massive cell death.
source: WT RNase L expression in RNASEL-ADAR1 DKO caused massive cell death while expression of inactive mutant RNase L did not.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4c and Videos 1-4.

claim: Expression of inactive mutant RNase L did not cause cell death in RNASEL-ADAR1 DKO cells.
source: WT RNase L expression in RNASEL-ADAR1 DKO caused massive cell death while expression of inactive mutant RNase L did not.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4c and Videos 1-4.

claim: Expression of WT or mutant RNase L had no effect on RNASE L KO cells with intact ADAR1.
source: Also, expression of WT or mutant RNase L had no effect on RNASE L KO cells with intact ADAR1.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4c and Videos 1-4.

claim: Murine coronavirus accessory protein NS2 has a 2',5'-phosphodiesterase (PDE) activity that cleaves 2-5A thereby antagonizing activation of RNase L.
source: To further demonstrate that endogenous dsRNA leads to RNase L activation thus accelerating cell death and that RNase L precludes recovery of ADAR1 KO cells, we constructed an A549 cell line expressing murine coronavirus accessory protein NS2 (NS2-WT), which has a 2',5'-phosphodiesterase (PDE) activity that cleaves 2-5A thereby antagonizing activation of RNase L.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Zhao et al., 2012.

claim: NS2H126R is an inactive mutant unable to antagonize RNase L due to loss of its ability to cleave 2-5A.
source: As a control, we also constructed a cell line expressing an inactive mutant NS2H126R, unable to antagonize RNase L due to loss of its ability to cleave 2-5A (Zhao et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Zhao et al., 2012.

claim: ADAR1 KO cells expressing functional NS2 PDE (NS2-ADAR1 KO) but not the inactive mutant PDE were recovered.
source: Using CRISPR/Cas9 engineering (sgRNAs 4) we were able to recover ADAR1 KO cells expressing functional NS2 PDE (NS2-ADAR1 KO) but not the inactive mutant PDE (Table 3, Figure 5a) indicating that antagonism of RNase L by NS2 mediated cleavage of 2-5A as well as RNASEL KO promotes recovery of ADAR1 KO cells.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Table 3 and Figure 5a.

claim: Antagonism of RNase L by NS2 mediated cleavage of 2-5A promotes recovery of ADAR1 KO cells.
source: Using CRISPR/Cas9 engineering (sgRNAs 4) we were able to recover ADAR1 KO cells expressing functional NS2 PDE (NS2-ADAR1 KO) but not the inactive mutant PDE (Table 3, Figure 5a) indicating that antagonism of RNase L by NS2 mediated cleavage of 2-5A as well as RNASEL KO promotes recovery of ADAR1 KO cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing that only functional NS2 allows recovery of ADAR1 KO cells.

claim: Transfection of NS2-ADAR1 KO cells with siRNA against NS2 reversed the NS2 phenotype, activated RNase L and promoted cell death by two days post-transfection.
source: Transfection of NS2-ADAR1 KO cells (clone C12) with siRNA against NS2 but not against control GFP reversed the NS2 phenotype, activated RNase L and promoted cell death by two days post-transfection while NS2-WT cells remained alive following siRNA mediated depletion of NS2 (Figure 5b and c).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5b and 5c.

claim: NS2-WT cells remained alive following siRNA mediated depletion of NS2.
source: Transfection of NS2-ADAR1 KO cells (clone C12) with siRNA against NS2 but not against control GFP reversed the NS2 phenotype, activated RNase L and promoted cell death by two days post-transfection while NS2-WT cells remained alive following siRNA mediated depletion of NS2 (Figure 5b and c).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5b and 5c.

claim: ADAR1 p150 isoform is responsible for the editing of RNA that activates MAVS or MDA5 in the mouse system.
source: Both of the these cell lines are deficient in expression of the ADAR1 p150 isoform (Figure 2a) previously reported in the mouse system to be responsible for the editing of RNA that activates MAVS or MDA5 (Pestal et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Pestal et al., 2015.

claim: Basal levels of 2-5A are minimal in the absence of exogenously added dsRNA.
source: Because basal levels of 2-5A are minimal in the absence of exogenously added dsRNA, and the consequent RNase L activity very low (Knight et al., 1980) we pre-treated cells with IFN to increase OAS protein levels prior to quantifying 2-5A accumulation and RNA degradation.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Knight et al., 1980.

claim: IFN treatment of ADAR1 KO cells upregulated ISG expression.
source: Indeed IFN treatment of ADAR1 KO cells upregulated ISG expression and further induced IFN by endogenous dsRNA in cells lacking expression of both isoforms of ADAR1 (p110 and p150) or ADAR1 p150 only (Figure 6).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6.

claim: IFN treatment of ADAR1 KO cells further induced IFN by endogenous dsRNA in cells lacking expression of both isoforms of ADAR1 (p110 and p150) or ADAR1 p150 only.
source: Indeed IFN treatment of ADAR1 KO cells upregulated ISG expression and further induced IFN by endogenous dsRNA in cells lacking expression of both isoforms of ADAR1 (p110 and p150) or ADAR1 p150 only (Figure 6).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6.

claim: IFN-induced accumulation of 2-5A was observed in RNASEL-ADAR1 DKO cells.
source: Using an indirect FRET based assay (Thakur et al., 2005) we observed IFN-induced accumulation of 2-5A in RNASEL-ADAR1 DKO and MAVS-ADAR1 DKO cells (although the latter not to a statistically significant extent) but not in WT, RNASEL KO or MAVS KO cells (Figure 7a).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7a.

claim: IFN-induced accumulation of 2-5A was observed in MAVS-ADAR1 DKO cells (although not to a statistically significant extent).
source: Using an indirect FRET based assay (Thakur et al., 2005) we observed IFN-induced accumulation of 2-5A in RNASEL-ADAR1 DKO and MAVS-ADAR1 DKO cells (although the latter not to a statistically significant extent) but not in WT, RNASEL KO or MAVS KO cells (Figure 7a).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7a.

claim: IFN-induced accumulation of 2-5A was not observed in WT, RNASEL KO or MAVS KO cells.
source: Using an indirect FRET based assay (Thakur et al., 2005) we observed IFN-induced accumulation of 2-5A in RNASEL-ADAR1 DKO and MAVS-ADAR1 DKO cells (although the latter not to a statistically significant extent) but not in WT, RNASEL KO or MAVS KO cells (Figure 7a).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7a.

claim: Highly specific and characteristic RNase L-mediated rRNA degradation products were observed in IFN treated ADAR1 p150 KO, MAVS-ADAR1 p150 DKO, or MAVS-ADAR1 DKO cells.
source: Furthermore, while rRNA remained intact in WT, RNASEL KO or MAVS KO cells, highly specific and characteristic RNase L-mediated rRNA degradation products (Silverman et al., 1983) identical to the pattern induced by Sindbis infection of WT A549 (Figure 7b) were observed by Bioanaylzer in IFN treated ADAR1 p150 KO, MAVS-ADAR1 p150 DKO, or MAVS-ADAR1 DKO cells.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7b and citation to Silverman et al., 1983.

claim: rRNA remained intact in WT, RNASEL KO or MAVS KO cells following IFN treatment.
source: Furthermore, while rRNA remained intact in WT, RNASEL KO or MAVS KO cells, highly specific and characteristic RNase L-mediated rRNA degradation products (Silverman et al., 1983) identical to the pattern induced by Sindbis infection of WT A549 (Figure 7b) were observed by Bioanaylzer in IFN treated ADAR1 p150 KO, MAVS-ADAR1 p150 DKO, or MAVS-ADAR1 DKO cells.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7b.

claim: 2-5A was produced and RNase L activated by endogenous RNA even in the absence of MAVS.
source: Thus 2-5A was produced and RNase L activated by endogenous RNA even in the absence of MAVS.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing 2-5A accumulation and rRNA degradation in MAVS-ADAR1 DKO cells.

claim: RNase L strongly and site-specifically cleaves tRNA-His at position 36 located in the anti-codon loop.
source: In addition to cleaving rRNA, RNase L was recently reported to strongly and site-specifically cleave tRNA-His at position 36 located in the anti-codon loop.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Donovan et al., 2016.

claim: Site-specific tRNA-His cleavage was readily observed in IFN-treated MAVS-ADAR1 DKO, but not in IFN-treated MAVS KO and RNASEL-ADAR1 DKO cells.
source: The site-specific tRNA-His cleavage was readily observed using a quantitative RT-PCR assay in IFN-treated MAVS-ADAR1 DKO, but not in IFN-treated cells, which lack RNase L activity in the above assays: MAVS KO andRNASEL-ADAR1 DKO cells (Figure 7c) (Donovan et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7c and citation to Donovan et al., 2016.

claim: Ablation of ADAR1 was previously shown to be lethal during mouse embryogenesis.
source: Ablation of ADAR1 was previously shown to be lethal during mouse embryogenesis (Pestal et al., 2015; Liddicoat et al., 2015; Mannion et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Pestal et al., 2015; Liddicoat et al., 2015; Mannion et al., 2014.

claim: Adar1 KO embryos show increased levels of IFN production and ISG expression relative to WT.
source: Adar1 KO embryos show increased levels of IFN production and ISG expression relative to WT and die by E12.5, implicating ADAR1 editing of dsRNA in regulating cell and animal survival.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies on Adar1 KO mice.

claim: Adar1 KO embryos die by E12.5.
source: Adar1 KO embryos show increased levels of IFN production and ISG expression relative to WT and die by E12.5, implicating ADAR1 editing of dsRNA in regulating cell and animal survival.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies on Adar1 KO mice.

claim: Deletion of MDA5 or MAVS overcomes ADAR1 deficiency and allows viability of mouse embryos.
source: However, deletion of MDA5 or MAVS, components of the canonical type I IFN production pathway (Figure 1), was shown to overcome the ADAR1 deficiency and allow the viability of mouse embryos, although most of the surviving mice died within the first few days after birth and there were abnormalities in organ development as well as excess IFN signaling (Pestal et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Pestal et al., 2015.

claim: Most of the surviving Adar1/Mda5 or Adar1/Mavs double KO mice died within the first few days after birth.
source: However, deletion of MDA5 or MAVS, components of the canonical type I IFN production pathway (Figure 1), was shown to overcome the ADAR1 deficiency and allow the viability of mouse embryos, although most of the surviving mice died within the first few days after birth and there were abnormalities in organ development as well as excess IFN signaling (Pestal et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Pestal et al., 2015.

claim: Adar1/Mda5 or Adar1/Mavs double KO mice had abnormalities in organ development as well as excess IFN signaling.
source: However, deletion of MDA5 or MAVS, components of the canonical type I IFN production pathway (Figure 1), was shown to overcome the ADAR1 deficiency and allow the viability of mouse embryos, although most of the surviving mice died within the first few days after birth and there were abnormalities in organ development as well as excess IFN signaling (Pestal et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Pestal et al., 2015.

claim: PKR ablation was unable to rescue Adar1 KO mouse embryo lethality.
source: While our finding that MAVS KO rescued the lethality of ADAR1 in a human cell system is consistent with the literature on Adar1 KO in murine systems in vivo and expected, the finding that RNase L ablation rescues the ADAR1 lethality even in the presence of MAVS and normal IFN response (Figure 2; Table 3) is unexpected. It is possible that, in the mouse embryo system, RNase L, activated downstream of MDA5-MAVS also contributes to embryonic lethality. However, rescue of lethality due to Adar1 KO by Mda5 or Mavs KO in the mouse embryo may be due to one or more other MAVS dependent activities. It should be noted that mouse embryo fibroblasts (mef) (Mannion et al., 2014) and HEK293T cells (Pestal et al., 2015) can survive ADAR1 KO.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Wang et al., 2004.

claim: Mouse embryo fibroblasts (mef) can survive ADAR1 KO.
source: It should be noted that mouse embryo fibroblasts (mef) (Mannion et al., 2014) and HEK293T cells (Pestal et al., 2015) can survive ADAR1 KO.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Mannion et al., 2014.

claim: HEK293T cells can survive ADAR1 KO.
source: It should be noted that mouse embryo fibroblasts (mef) (Mannion et al., 2014) and HEK293T cells (Pestal et al., 2015) can survive ADAR1 KO.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Pestal et al., 2015.

claim: Mouse embryo fibroblasts and HEK293T cells can survive ADAR1 KO likely due to low levels of OAS expression.
source: This is likely due to the low levels of OAS expression in these cell types (Banerjee et al., 2014) (and data not shown) and in the case of mefs, also a low level of RNase L (Banerjee et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Banerjee et al., 2014 and inference from the data.

claim: Mouse embryo fibroblasts have low levels of RNase L.
source: This is likely due to the low levels of OAS expression in these cell types (Banerjee et al., 2014) (and data not shown) and in the case of mefs, also a low level of RNase L (Banerjee et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Banerjee et al., 2014.

claim: Ectopic expression of active RNase L, but not mutant inactive RNase L, promotes death of ADAR1 deficient cells.
source: The observation that ectopic expression of active RNase L, but not mutant inactive RNase L, promotes death of ADAR1 deficient cells supports the central role of RNase L activation in dsRNA-mediated cell death (Figure 4c, Videos 1–4).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4c and Videos 1-4.

claim: Expression of the MHV PDE, NS2, a potent RNase L antagonist, but not its inactive mutant, enables recovery of viable ADAR1 KO cells.
source: Further supporting this conclusion, expression of the MHV PDE, NS2, a potent RNase L antagonist (Zhao et al., 2012), but not its inactive mutant, enables recovery of viable ADAR1 KO cells while knockdown of NS2 in ADAR1 KO cells leads to cell death (Figure 5).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5 and citation to Zhao et al., 2012.

claim: Knockdown of NS2 in ADAR1 KO cells leads to cell death.
source: Further supporting this conclusion, expression of the MHV PDE, NS2, a potent RNase L antagonist (Zhao et al., 2012), but not its inactive mutant, enables recovery of viable ADAR1 KO cells while knockdown of NS2 in ADAR1 KO cells leads to cell death (Figure 5).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: RNase L has a predominant role in promoting cell death by dsRNA.
source: Based on these results, we propose that RNase L has a predominant role in promoting cell death by dsRNA (Figure 1).
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental results showing that RNase L ablation provides the strongest protection against dsRNA-induced cell death.

claim: RNase L site-specifically cleaves tRNAs and Y-RNAs.
source: It has been shown recently that RNase L site-specifically cleaves tRNAs and Y-RNAs, and that depletion of the Y-RNA RNY1 contributes to apoptosis (Donovan et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Donovan et al., 2016.

claim: Depletion of the Y-RNA RNY1 contributes to apoptosis.
source: It has been shown recently that RNase L site-specifically cleaves tRNAs and Y-RNAs, and that depletion of the Y-RNA RNY1 contributes to apoptosis (Donovan et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Donovan et al., 2016.

claim: Deletion of PKR did not allow recovery of ADAR1 KO cells.
source: In contrast to RNase L, and consistent with mouse embryo studies (Wang et al., 2004), deletion of PKR did not allow recovery of ADAR1 KO cells and single PKR KO did not change the kinetics of pIC-induced death in cells that contained ADAR1 (Table 3, Figure 3).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Table 3 and Figure 3, and citation to Wang et al., 2004.

claim: Single PKR KO did not change the kinetics of pIC-induced death in cells that contained ADAR1.
source: In contrast to RNase L, and consistent with mouse embryo studies (Wang et al., 2004), deletion of PKR did not allow recovery of ADAR1 KO cells and single PKR KO did not change the kinetics of pIC-induced death in cells that contained ADAR1 (Table 3, Figure 3).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Table 3 and Figure 3.

claim: PKR does not substantially contribute to ADAR1 KO cell lethality.
source: Apparently, PKR (a dsRNA-activated protein kinase that inhibits translation) does not substantially contribute to ADAR1 KO cell lethality.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing that PKR KO does not rescue ADAR1 deficiency.

claim: PKR was activated by pIC in WT A549 cells resulting in phosphorylation of eIF2α.
source: [PKR was activated by pIC in WT A549 cells resulting in phosphorylation of eIF2α, whereas pIC treatment of PKR KO cells did not result in phosphorylated eIF2α, (Figure 2d).]
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2d.

claim: pIC treatment of PKR KO cells did not result in phosphorylated eIF2α.
source: [PKR was activated by pIC in WT A549 cells resulting in phosphorylation of eIF2α, whereas pIC treatment of PKR KO cells did not result in phosphorylated eIF2α, (Figure 2d).]
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2d.

claim: IFN treatment of ADAR1 deficient cells did not induce PKR expression, in contrast to ADAR1 expressing cells.
source: However, it is noted that IFN treatment of ADAR1 deficient cells did not induce PKR expression, in contrast to ADAR1 expressing cells (Figure 2a, Figure 5a, Figure 2—source data 2–source data1; Figure 5—source data 5–source data1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2a and Figure 5a.

claim: Endogenous cellular dsRNA activates OAS leading to RNase L activity in MAVS-ADAR1 KO cells.
source: Endogenous cellular dsRNA activates OAS leading to RNase L activity in MAVS-ADAR1 KO cells as evidenced by rRNA degradation, site-specific tRNA-His cleavage following IFN stimulation, and accumulation of 2-5A in RNASEL KO cells, even in the absence of exogenous dsRNA (Figure 7).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7.

claim: dsRNA is the only well-established activator of OAS enzymatic activity.
source: It should be noted that dsRNA is the only well-established activator of OAS enzymatic activity [ Silverman and Weiss, 2014 and references therein].
evidence: This is supported by citation to Silverman and Weiss, 2014.

claim: IFN treatment of RNASEL-ADAR1 DKO cells produces enhanced expression of IFN-β and -λ, and ISGs.
source: While IFN treatment of RNASEL-ADAR1 DKO cells produces enhanced expression of IFN-β and -λ, and ISGs, these effects of IFN were reduced in MAVS-ADAR1 DKO cells.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6.

claim: The effects of IFN on expression of IFN-β and -λ, and ISGs were reduced in MAVS-ADAR1 DKO cells.
source: While IFN treatment of RNASEL-ADAR1 DKO cells produces enhanced expression of IFN-β and -λ, and ISGs, these effects of IFN were reduced in MAVS-ADAR1 DKO cells.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6.

claim: MAVS is likely to augment RNase L activation through the upregulation of IFNs and OASs.
source: Our findings suggest that MAVS is likely to augment RNase L activation through the upregulation of IFNs and OASs (which are ISGs), effects that do not require exogenous dsRNA when ADAR1 is deficient (Figure 6).
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing enhanced ISG expression in RNASEL-ADAR1 DKO vs MAVS-ADAR1 DKO cells.

claim: The accumulation of 2-5A was greater in MAVS-ADAR1 DKO cells compared to MAVS (although not statistically significant).
source: Indeed, although not statistically significant, the accumulation of 2-5A was greater in MAVS-ADAR1 DKO cells compared to MAVS (Figure 7).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7a.

claim: Deletion of MAVS promotes the viability of A549 cells engineered to lack ADAR1.
source: Moreover, deletion of MAVS promotes the viability of A549 cells engineered to lack ADAR1 and upon pIC treatment, the MAVS KO cells exhibit a slower rate of cell death than WT A549 (Figure 3).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3 and Table 3.

claim: Upon pIC treatment, MAVS KO cells exhibit a slower rate of cell death than WT A549.
source: Moreover, deletion of MAVS promotes the viability of A549 cells engineered to lack ADAR1 and upon pIC treatment, the MAVS KO cells exhibit a slower rate of cell death than WT A549 (Figure 3).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: MAVS-ADAR1 DKO cells die faster than RNASEL-ADAR1 DKO cells most likely because RNase L can be activated in the former cells.
source: Nevertheless, MAVS-ADAR1 DKO cells die faster than RNASEL-ADAR1 DKO cells most likely because RNase L can be activated in the former cells (Figure 4a; Figure 7b and c).
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing RNase L activity in MAVS-ADAR1 DKO cells.

claim: RNase L can be activated in the absence of MAVS expression in MAVS-ADAR1 DKO cells by pIC.
source: Thus, while the MDA5/MAVS pathway plays a central role in IFN induction and signaling and can upregulate both OAS and PKR (Figure 1), these data indicate that RNase L can be activated in the absence of MAVS expression in MAVS-ADAR1 DKO cells by pIC.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing RNase L activation in MAVS-ADAR1 DKO cells treated with pIC.

claim: Activation of RNase L during virus infections does not depend on IFN induction.
source: These results are consistent with our previous findings that activation of RNase L during virus infections does not depend on IFN induction (Birdwell et al., 2016; Li et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Birdwell et al., 2016; Li et al., 2016.

claim: RNase L-induced cell death could potentially contribute to symptoms of Aicardi-Goutiéres syndrome in cases with mutation of ADAR1.
source: Since RNase L is activated in the absence of ADAR1 editing contributing to cell death, RNase L-induced cell death could potentially contribute to symptoms of the neurodegenerative and inflammatory disease Aicardi-Goutiéres syndrome (AGS) in cases with mutation of ADAR1 (Rice et al., 2012).
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the experimental findings and citation to Rice et al., 2012.

claim: Mutations of genes responsible for AGS, such as RNase H2, led to self-DNA-mediated activation of cGAS in mouse models.
source: In mouse models, mutations of genes responsible for AGS, such as RNase H2 (Pokatayev et al., 2016) and Trex1 (Gray et al., 2015), led to self-DNA-mediated activation of cGAS, a protein functionally and structurally similar to OASs (Hornung et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Pokatayev et al., 2016; Gray et al., 2015; Hornung et al., 2014.

claim: Mutations of Trex1 led to self-DNA-mediated activation of cGAS in mouse models.
source: In mouse models, mutations of genes responsible for AGS, such as RNase H2 (Pokatayev et al., 2016) and Trex1 (Gray et al., 2015), led to self-DNA-mediated activation of cGAS, a protein functionally and structurally similar to OASs (Hornung et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Gray et al., 2015; Hornung et al., 2014.

claim: cGAS is a protein functionally and structurally similar to OASs.
source: In mouse models, mutations of genes responsible for AGS, such as RNase H2 (Pokatayev et al., 2016) and Trex1 (Gray et al., 2015), led to self-DNA-mediated activation of cGAS, a protein functionally and structurally similar to OASs (Hornung et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Hornung et al., 2014.

claim: Mutation of ADAR1 leads to self-dsRNA activation of one or more OAS isoform resulting in RNase L activity and cell death.
source: Our findings show that mutation of ADAR1 leads to self-dsRNA activation of one or more OAS isoform resulting in RNase L activity and cell death.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data showing OAS activation and RNase L activity in ADAR1 deficient cells.

claim: Mutations affecting homologous nucleic acid sensors in the IFN system, cGAS and OAS, both of which produce unusual 2'−5' internucleotide linkages, lead to AGS although through different signaling pathways.
source: We suggest that mutations affecting homologous nucleic acid sensors in the IFN system, cGAS and OAS, both of which produce unusual 2'−5' internucleotide linkages, lead to AGS although through different signaling pathways.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the experimental findings and comparison with other AGS-causing mutations.

claim: Presence of RNase L contributed to secretion of the pro-inflammatory cytokine IL-1β in virus-infected mice.
source: In vivo evidence for the pro-inflammatory role of RNase L was obtained in virus-infected mice where presence of RNase L contributed to secretion of the pro-inflammatory cytokine IL-1β (Chakrabarti et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Chakrabarti et al., 2015.

claim: An RNase L inhibitor drug could potentially reduce tissue damage and alleviate inflammation in some circumstances.
source: Therefore, an RNase L inhibitor drug could potentially reduce tissue damage and alleviate inflammation in some circumstances.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the findings about RNase L's role in cell death and inflammation.
